summary: Gives a framework for deploying IP multicast in an MPLS environment. It describes issues in applying MPLS to multicast, the pros and cons of existing multicast routing protocols in that setting, and how different layer 2 technologies and label distribution approaches affect it.

plainLanguage.summary: Sending one video to many viewers is tricky when your network moves traffic using labels. This overview explains the trouble spots and choices of mixing the two.

subtitle: How to efficiently route one-to-many communications in a label-switched network

tldr.problem: Applying MPLS label switching to IP multicast creates complexity: different multicast routing protocols create different tree structures, MPLS label limitations affect how many simultaneous streams can be supported, and layer 2 technologies like ATM impose merging constraints.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes a framework for IP multicast in MPLS by categorizing multicast routing protocols by their characteristics (flood & prune, source vs. shared trees, etc.), addressing how to handle state coexistence, and considering different label distribution trigger methods and layer 2 impacts.
tldr.outcome: Network designers can choose approaches to multicast over MPLS based on their topology, protocols, and performance needs, with trade-offs between label consumption, forwarding complexity, and latency.

today: RFC 3353 is Informational and provides a framework for understanding IP multicast in MPLS environments. It has not been obsoleted and remains a reference for network designers implementing multicast over label-switched networks.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: The Multi-Protocol Label Switching (MPLS) protocol maps Layer 3 routing paths onto Layer 2 paths to enhance network performance and enable services like Quality of Service and traffic engineering. MPLS enhances unicast routing, where the optimal shortest path is typically the same across protocols. However, IP multicast is more complex: different multicast protocols generate different tree structures, and no current protocol maintains an optimal Steiner tree (the minimum cost tree connecting N nodes). This document addresses the issues that arise when MPLS label switching is applied to IP multicast within a single domain.
sections.plainLanguage: MPLS uses labels to make routing faster. Regular (unicast) routing is straightforward—there is usually one best path. With multicast, one sender sends to many receivers and different protocols create different paths, making MPLS more complicated.

sections.title: Layer 2 Limitations
sections.content:
MPLS runs on top of several Layer 2 technologies such as PPP, Ethernet, ATM, and Frame Relay. ATM is particularly relevant because it offers high switching capacity and quality-of-service awareness, but it creates three significant limitations when used with MPLS multicast.

Limited label space: ATM's VPI/VCI fields and Frame Relay's DLCI space have small bit allocations, limiting the number of Label Switched Paths (LSPs) that can exist simultaneously. Merging: some Layer 2 technologies do not support multipoint-to-multipoint connections, preventing multiple multicast streams from merging onto a single LSP. TTL handling: Layer 2 technologies do not decrement the IP TTL field, potentially causing infinite forwarding loops if not handled carefully. Native MPLS over Ethernet or PPP avoids these limitations and allows the same label to be reused for both unicast and multicast LSPs using different EtherTypes.
sections.plainLanguage: When MPLS uses ATM or Frame Relay, there are problems: not enough label slots, inability to combine multiple streams, and trouble with time-to-live counting. Ethernet does not have these problems.

sections.title: Multicast Routing Protocol Characteristics
sections.content:
Different IP multicast routing protocols have different characteristics relevant to MPLS. Flood and Prune protocols (like DVMRP and PIM-DM) initially flood the network and then remove unnecessary branches, creating volatile tree structures that consume many labels. Source trees (S, G) create one tree per source and group pair, while shared trees (*, G) create one tree per group, using fewer labels but requiring complex multipoint-to-multipoint merging.

PIM-SM uniquely supports both source and shared trees simultaneously, creating state coexistence challenges: when traffic switches from a shared tree to a source tree, some routers temporarily have both states for the same group. Handling this coexistence in label switching requires careful design—either returning to layer 3 forwarding, using source-specific labels on shared trees, label-switching only source trees, or creating dedicated LSPs for (S, G) traffic merged onto (*, G) LSPs. Bidirectional shared trees (like CBT) create many merging points as multiple sources feed into the tree, while unidirectional trees tunnel source traffic to a root, reducing merging complexity.
sections.plainLanguage: Some multicast protocols flood everywhere then prune unneeded paths (wasteful). Others build trees per source (many labels) or per group (fewer labels but complex). Some do both at once, which is tricky to handle with labels.

sections.title: Mixed Layer 2 and Layer 3 Forwarding
sections.content: Unicast traffic has one incoming and one outgoing interface, so it is forwarded either at Layer 2 (via label switching) or at Layer 3 (via IP routing). Multicast traffic can be forwarded to multiple outgoing interfaces, enabling hybrid approaches: some branches are forwarded at Layer 2 via LSP while others are forwarded at Layer 3. Nodes supporting mixed L2/L3 forwarding use an extra bit in the Multicast Routing Table to prevent traffic from being forwarded on branches that already received it via Layer 2.
sections.plainLanguage: With multicast, you can send copies to multiple places at once. Some copies can travel by fast labels (Layer 2) while others take the regular IP path (Layer 3) from the same router.

sections.title: LSP Trigger Methods
sections.content: Creating LSPs for multicast can be triggered in different ways. Request-driven triggers respond to multicast routing messages or resource reservation messages, establishing LSPs on demand. Topology-driven triggers create LSPs based on the multicast routing table structure. Traffic-driven triggers establish LSPs when data actually arrives for a group, which is natural for flood-and-prune protocols but adds setup latency. The choice of trigger method (request-driven, topology-driven, or traffic-driven) affects performance, label consumption, and forwarding efficiency, and must be considered alongside the label distribution mode (upstream or downstream).
sections.plainLanguage: An LSP can be created when a request asks for it, when the routing table changes, or when actual traffic shows up. Different choices have different trade-offs.

sections.title: Advanced Considerations
sections.content: Several additional issues affect multicast MPLS deployment. Piggy-backing of multicast data with label distribution messages can reduce overhead. Explicit routing allows manual control of multicast paths. Quality of Service handling via DiffServ or IntServ must be carefully designed, as multicast creates different CoS requirements for different branches. Multi-access networks (like Ethernet LANs) require special consideration for designated routers and label distribution. Loop prevention is critical because multicast packets looping in a network generate exponential copies as branches exist in the loop, though loop detection mechanisms remain configurable options. Label retention mode (conservative vs. liberal), label distribution control (independent vs. ordered), and label allocation (downstream vs. upstream) also influence system behavior.
sections.plainLanguage: Other tricky details: preventing loops is critical because loop copies multiply, handling QoS for different branches, managing many routers on a shared network, and deciding who allocates labels and when.
